fig01_metric_function.name: fig01_metric_function
fig01_metric_function.caption: Schwarzschild metric function f(r) (left). The component g_rr = 1/f diverges at the horizon in Schwarzschild coordinates but the determinant of the (v, r) block of the ingoing Eddington-Finkelstein metric equals -c^2 everywhere, so the horizon is a coordinate artefact there (right).

fig02_kretschmann_scalar.name: fig02_kretschmann_scalar
fig02_kretschmann_scalar.caption: K = 12 r_s^2 / r^6 = 48 G^2 M^2 / (c^4 r^6), verified symbolically (tests/test_spacetimes.py). K is finite at r = r_s, so the horizon is not a curvature singularity; K diverges only at r = 0.

fig03_tortoise_coordinate.name: fig03_tortoise_coordinate
fig03_tortoise_coordinate.caption: r_* = r + r_s ln(r/r_s - 1). Fitted slope d(r_*/r_s)/d ln(r/r_s - 1) for r/r_s - 1 < 1e-4 is 1.000003 (expected 1). The horizon is infinitely far away in r_*, which underlies the mode definitions used for Hawking radiation.

fig04_radial_null_rays.name: fig04_radial_null_rays
fig04_radial_null_rays.caption: Radial null geodesics t = t0 +/- (r_*(r) - r_*(r0))/c in Schwarzschild time. Rays approach r = r_s only asymptotically in t, illustrating the coordinate singularity of Schwarzschild time at the horizon.

fig05_hawking_temperature.name: fig05_hawking_temperature
fig05_hawking_temperature.caption: Hawking temperature versus mass for Schwarzschild black holes. A black hole is hotter than the 2.725 K CMB only below about 4.5e+22 kg; stellar-mass holes (T ~ 1e-7 K) absorb more than they radiate in the present universe.

fig06_entropy_vs_mass.name: fig06_entropy_vs_mass
fig06_entropy_vs_mass.caption: Bekenstein-Hawking entropy S_BH = 4 pi k_B G M^2/(hbar c). Fitted log-log slope 2.00000000; the ratio of the closed form to A/(4 l_P^2) deviates from 1 by at most 4.4e-16 (floating-point round-off).

fig07_first_law_residual.name: fig07_first_law_residual
fig07_first_law_residual.caption: Relative residual of the first law of black-hole mechanics evaluated with central finite differences of the analytic M(S, Q, J). The residual follows the O(h^2) truncation error at large steps and is limited by round-off at small steps (the Schwarzschild entropy is exactly quadratic in M, so it is dominated by round-off throughout).

fig08_heat_capacity_stability.name: fig08_heat_capacity_stability
fig08_heat_capacity_stability.caption: Heat capacities in their stated ensembles. Schwarzschild: C = -2 S_BH < 0 (local thermodynamic instability). RN at fixed charge: positive for r_+ < sqrt(3)|Q| (near-extremal), diverging and negative beyond. Schwarzschild-AdS at fixed L: negative for r_+ < L/sqrt(3) (small BH), positive for large BH. Local thermodynamic stability is distinct from global preference (Fig 09) and from dynamical stability, which is not analysed here.

fig09_free_energy_hawking_page.name: fig09_free_energy_hawking_page
fig09_free_energy_hawking_page.caption: Free energy of Schwarzschild-AdS black holes (large branch solid, small branch dashed) compared with thermal AdS (F = 0). Black holes exist only above T_min = sqrt(3)/(2 pi L); the large branch crosses F = 0 at T_HP = 1/(pi L) (r_+ = L), reproducing the Hawking-Page transition (Hawking and Page 1983). Asymptotically flat Schwarzschild has F = M/2 > 0 at all temperatures and no preferred equilibrium (negative heat capacity).

fig10_extremal_limits.name: fig10_extremal_limits
fig10_extremal_limits.caption: Temperature, entropy and horizon angular velocity as functions of charge-to-mass ratio (RN) and spin (Kerr), normalised to the Schwarzschild values at equal M. T vanishes continuously at extremality with finite entropy; the Kerr Smarr relation M = 2TS + 2 Omega J holds to round-off (tests/test_spacetimes.py). The horizon radius is computed as sqrt((M-Q)(M+Q)) to avoid cancellation near extremality.

fig11_evaporation.name: fig11_evaporation
fig11_evaporation.caption: Quasi-static photon-only evaporation (L = sigma_SB A T_H^4, no greybody factors or other species): numerical integration vs the closed form, lifetime scaling and the adiabaticity parameter epsilon = (hbar/k_B T_H)|dM/dt|/M. The photon-only lifetime equals the age of the universe at M ~ 1.73e+11 kg. These lifetimes are approximations. epsilon grows as M^-2 but is still only 5.2e-04 at the Planck mass (it reaches 0.1 at 0.07 M_P), so this heuristic criterion does not locate the breakdown of the semiclassical picture; Planck-scale effects are expected earlier and are not modelled. The model is not extended to the endpoint.

fig12_entropy_vs_area_log_correction.name: fig12_entropy_vs_area_log_correction
fig12_entropy_vs_area_log_correction.caption: Bekenstein-Hawking entropy with a parameterised logarithmic correction. The coefficient alpha is model dependent and the three values shown are illustrative only (different microscopic approaches give different values; none is assumed here). The fitted slope of the correction against ln A recovers alpha = -1.500000 for the alpha = -3/2 curve.

fig13_area_vs_volume_scaling.name: fig13_area_vs_volume_scaling
fig13_area_vs_volume_scaling.caption: An ordinary thermal system (photon gas at fixed temperature) has extensive entropy S ~ R^3, whereas the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy of a black hole of radius R scales as R^2. At 300 K the crossover lies at R ~ 1.5e54 m, far beyond the observable universe (4.4e26 m), so the plot illustrates only the different scaling exponents, not a bound; it does not identify the black-hole microstates.

fig14_ensembles_finite_vs_gravitating.name: fig14_ensembles_finite_vs_gravitating
fig14_ensembles_finite_vs_gravitating.caption: (a) Heat capacity of finite two-level systems computed directly from the density of states (binomial degeneracies) and compared with the closed form; it is non-negative in the canonical ensemble. (b) For S(E) = 4 pi E^2 the exponent S(E) - beta E of the canonical integral has its stationary point at E = beta/(8 pi), which is a minimum (second derivative 8 pi > 0): the canonical integral does not converge as a dominated saddle and the canonical and microcanonical descriptions disagree (Planck units, k_B = 1).

fig15_hawking_spectra.name: fig15_hawking_spectra
fig15_hawking_spectra.caption: (a) Bose-Einstein and Fermi-Dirac occupation as functions of x = hbar omega/(k_B T_H). (b) Photon-only blackbody spectra with the horizon area for three masses; the peak sits near x = 2.82 (Wien, in terms of dP/domega) and moves to lower energy as M grows. A thermal curve illustrates the spectrum; it is not a derivation of Hawking radiation (see docs/hawking_radiation.md), and greybody factors (Figs 18-20) modify it.

fig16_effective_potentials.name: fig16_effective_potentials
fig16_effective_potentials.caption: Effective potentials V = f [l(l+1)/r^2 + (1 - s^2) r_s/r^3] for massless fields of spin s = 0, 1, 2 (units r_s = 1). The barrier peak lies near the photon sphere and rises like l(l+1); the scattering of waves off it determines the greybody factor. All potentials vanish at the horizon and decay as l(l+1)/r^2 at infinity.

fig17_greybody_factors.name: fig17_greybody_factors
fig17_greybody_factors.caption: Transmission probabilities obtained by integrating the radial wave equation from the horizon (pure ingoing wave) to a large radius and decomposing into Riccati-Hankel waves. All values lie in [0, 1] and Wronskian flux conservation holds to 1e-09 (relative to the incident flux). Low multipoles transmit well above y ~ 0.3 while high multipoles are suppressed by the centrifugal barrier. Spin-1 and spin-2 fields have a stronger barrier at the same l.

fig18_absorption_cross_section.name: fig18_absorption_cross_section
fig18_absorption_cross_section.caption: Absorption cross-section of the Schwarzschild black hole for a massless scalar from the computed transmission probabilities. It tends to the horizon area as omega -> 0 (Das, Gibbons and Mathur 1997) and oscillates around the geometric-optics value (27/4) pi r_s^2 at high frequency (Sanchez 1978). Adding one further multipole changes sigma by at most 9.2e-11 (relative) over the range.

fig19_emission_rate_greybody.name: fig19_emission_rate_greybody
fig19_emission_rate_greybody.caption: d^2N/(dt d omega) = (1/2 pi) sum (2l+1) Gamma_l / (exp(hbar omega/k_B T_H) - 1) for a single real scalar, computed from the transmission probabilities, compared with blackbody emission from the horizon area and from the geometric-optics capture area. At low frequency the s-wave reproduces the horizon-area blackbody; the integrated scalar power is 7.19 times the horizon-area blackbody power for one bosonic degree of freedom (the geometric-optics blackbody, with emitting area 4 pi b_c^2 = 27 pi r_s^2, gives 27/4 = 6.75 and is reproduced numerically).

fig20_bell_and_product_entropies.name: fig20_bell_and_product_entropies
fig20_bell_and_product_entropies.caption: (a) Single-qubit entropy of cos(t)|00> + sin(t)|11>: zero for the product state, ln 2 for the Bell state, while the global entropy is zero throughout. (b) Product state: all quantities vanish. Bell state: S(AB) = 0, S(A) = ln 2, I = 2 ln 2, N = 1/2. Classically correlated mixture: I = ln 2 but N = 0 (correlation without entanglement). Werner state p = 0.5: mixed, entangled.

fig21_density_matrix_eigenvalues.name: fig21_density_matrix_eigenvalues
fig21_density_matrix_eigenvalues.caption: Eigenvalue distributions of random density matrices. (a) Hilbert-Schmidt measure (G G^dagger normalised, square Ginibre G) for d = 64 follows the Marchenko-Pastur law with c = 1 (support [0, 4]). (b) The reduced state of a Haar-random 16 x 64 bipartite pure state follows Marchenko-Pastur with c = m/n = 1/4 (support [1/4, 9/4]); the gap at zero is the signature of a subsystem much smaller than its complement (Page regime).

fig22_density_matrix_gallery.name: fig22_density_matrix_gallery
fig22_density_matrix_gallery.caption: Magnitudes |rho_ij| of two-qubit density matrices in the computational basis, with global entropy S, single-qubit entropy S(A) and purity Tr(rho^2) in the panel titles. The Bell state has off-diagonal coherences between |00> and |11>; the separable mixture has coherences too but is not entangled (negativity 0).

fig23_mutual_information_purity.name: fig23_mutual_information_purity
fig23_mutual_information_purity.caption: Werner states. Mutual information is non-zero for every p > 0 (it counts classical and quantum correlations) whereas negativity and concurrence vanish for p <= 1/3 (computed threshold on the grid: p = 0.335). Purity decreases monotonically as p decreases; the global entropy is 0 only at p = 1.

fig24_thermofield_pair_entropy.name: fig24_thermofield_pair_entropy
fig24_thermofield_pair_entropy.caption: Truncated two-mode squeezed (Bogoliubov-pair) state |Psi> = sqrt(1-q) sum_n q^{n/2}|n>_in|n>_out with q = exp(-hbar omega/k_B T_H). The global state is pure; tracing out the interior gives the thermal Bose distribution with <n> = 1/(e^x - 1) and entropy (n+1)ln(n+1) - n ln n. d = 2 reproduces the large-x limit (a qubit) only. Convergence in d is geometric, faster at large x. This models the mode structure, not the near-horizon field dynamics that produce it.

fig25_pair_emission_model.name: fig25_pair_emission_model
fig25_pair_emission_model.caption: N = 8 independent horizon pairs. Radiation R_k is the first k outgoing qubits; the interior holds all N partners. S(R_k) = k S_pair and I(R_k:interior) = 2 S(R_k): the emission entropy grows monotonically because the model never lets the radiation interact with the interior, i.e. it encodes the semiclassical (Hawking) assumption and has no mechanism to return information. Compare Figs 28-31, where unitary dynamics among the remaining degrees of freedom produces a turnover.

fig26_lattice_entanglement.name: fig26_lattice_entanglement
fig26_lattice_entanglement.caption: Ground-state entanglement entropy of a block of the massless-limit harmonic chain (Gaussian state, symplectic spectrum of the block covariance). (a) The slope against ln[(N/pi) sin(pi l/N)] is 0.2970, about 11% below the CFT value c/3 = 1/3 (c = 1). The deficit is an infrared effect: the correlation length 1/(ma) = 1000 sites is only 3.9 times the chain length, and diagnostics outside this script show the fitted slope falls further for larger ma (about 0.14 at ma = 0.01, N = 256) and approaches 1/3 as m N -> 0. (b) At fixed physical size the entropy grows as 0.3333 ln(1/a): the lattice spacing regulates the ultraviolet divergence. (c) Dirichlet/Neumann ends change the entropy of an end block (one entangling point instead of two) but not the interior block far from the boundary. (d) The IR mass lowers the entropy; finite-size corrections shrink as N grows. This is a lattice-field result, not a black-hole entropy calculation.

fig27_page_curves_dimensions.name: fig27_page_curves_dimensions
fig27_page_curves_dimensions.caption: Haar-average entropy of the first k of N qubits from Page's exact formula <S_{m,n}> = psi(mn+1) - psi(n+1) - (m-1)/(2n). The normalised curves approach the piecewise-linear bound min(k, N-k)/N as N grows (the rise-then-fall shape comes from sampling pure states of a fixed total dimension, not from an imposed curve). At the symmetric point the average falls short of the maximal value (N/2) ln 2 by 1/2 nat in the large-N limit (b).

fig28_page_curve_ensembles.name: fig28_page_curve_ensembles
fig28_page_curve_ensembles.caption: Ensemble of Haar-random pure states of N qubits; S(R_k) is the entropy of the first k qubits. Dark band: +/- 2 standard errors of the mean (this is the Monte Carlo error); light band: +/- 1 sample standard deviation (the genuine state-to-state fluctuation, which shrinks as N grows). The Monte Carlo mean agrees with the exact average within the statistical error. Results are reproducible for the seeds recorded in the figure sidecar.

fig29_hawking_vs_page_reference.name: fig29_hawking_vs_page_reference
fig29_hawking_vs_page_reference.caption: The monotonic semiclassical reference S = k ln 2 (each emitted quantum is maximally entangled with a partner that stays out of reach) violates the dimension bound for k > N/2. The entropy of the radiation in any globally pure state of the finite system must turn over at or before the Page point, because S(R) = S(B) <= (N-k) ln 2.

fig30_renyi_entropy_vs_index.name: fig30_renyi_entropy_vs_index
fig30_renyi_entropy_vs_index.caption: Renyi entropies of four d = 8 states computed from the eigenvalues. S_0 = ln rank, S_1 is the von Neumann entropy (markers), S_2 = -ln Tr rho^2 and S_infinity = -ln lambda_max. The curves are non-increasing in n and flat only for the maximally mixed state, whose spectrum is flat.

fig31_replica_vs_direct_entropy.name: fig31_replica_vs_direct_entropy
fig31_replica_vs_direct_entropy.caption: Replica identity for a random d = 8 density matrix (S_vN = 1.503146). (a) ln Tr rho^n and its tangent at n = 1. (b) Finite-difference error: quadratic in h for the central difference and quartic for Richardson down to a round-off floor of ~1e-10..1e-11. (c) In finite dimension the continuation from integer replicas alone (polynomial interpolation) converges only slowly; gravitational path integrals provide only integer-n data, which is why the analytic continuation is the hard step there. A finite-dimensional calculation is not a gravitational path integral.

fig32_unitary_vs_nonunitary_evaporation.name: fig32_unitary_vs_nonunitary_evaporation
fig32_unitary_vs_nonunitary_evaporation.caption: Toy evaporation of an N = 10 qubit register: each step applies a Haar-random unitary to the remaining black-hole qubits and then emits one qubit. (a) Unitary evolution reproduces the Page curve (mean over 24 seeds vs the exact average); the non-unitary reference (each emitted qubit is traced out of a mixed register and discarded from correlations) gives the monotonic Hawking-like S(R) = k ln 2. (b) The unitary global state stays pure (max norm deviation 8.9e-16); the non-unitary one becomes mixed. (c) The mutual information between radiation and black hole is 2 S(R) in the unitary model and zero in the reference. Non-unitary averages use 4 seeds. This is a qubit toy model, not a gravitational calculation.

fig33_entanglement_spectrum_evolution.name: fig33_entanglement_spectrum_evolution
fig33_entanglement_spectrum_evolution.caption: Entanglement spectrum of the radiation for one seed of the unitary toy. The number of nonzero eigenvalues is bounded by min(2^k, 2^(N-k)); the effective rank exp(S) follows it up to the Page point and then decreases, which is the spectral statement of the Page turnover.

fig34_generalized_entropy_branches.name: fig34_generalized_entropy_branches
fig34_generalized_entropy_branches.caption: Phenomenological island toy model S_gen(u) = S_H(1 + mu u) + S_rad exp(-u/xi) with S_H = S0 (1-tau)^(2/3) and S_rad = r (S0 - S_H); parameters S0 = 1000, r = 1.333, mu = 1, xi = 0.05. (a) The island candidate is a minimum of S_gen in u (dots). (b) The entropy of the radiation is the smaller of the no-island and island branches; the switch at tau_P = 0.6203 is a kink, i.e. a first-order-like transition. (c) After tau_P the radiation entropy follows the black-hole entropy. The functional form and parameters are illustrative assumptions, not derived from gravity.

fig35_island_parameter_study.name: fig35_island_parameter_study
fig35_island_parameter_study.caption: (a) Bounded-minimiser and closed-form island locations agree to ~1e-8 (max difference in S_gen 1.1e-13). (b) Page time of the toy model against the entropy ratio r for several xi; xi (through kappa = mu xi) shifts it only slightly from the kappa -> 0 closed form 1 - (r/(1+r))^(3/2). (c) The normalised curve depends weakly on S0, so the shape is set by r and xi. All parameters are illustrative.

fig36_holographic_entropy_ads3_btz.name: fig36_holographic_entropy_ads3_btz
fig36_holographic_entropy_ads3_btz.caption: Ryu-Takayanagi lengths with L = 1, G_N = 1. (a) The closed-form Poincare AdS3 geodesic length and a numerical quadrature of the semicircle agree. (b) In BTZ the connected geodesic competes with the horizon-wrapping candidate; they cross at Delta phi = 5.5919 (the cutoff cancels). The minimum encodes the Araki-Lieb behaviour S(A) - S(A^c) = (horizon length)/4G. (c) Entropy S = min(length)/4G_N; the kink marks the switch to the horizon-wrapping candidate and moves toward 2 pi as r_+ increases (about 5.59 at r_+ = 1), so for large r_+ the entropy is the connected-geodesic (extensive thermal) result over almost the whole circle. An independent turning-radius integration reproduces the connected closed form to 1.2e-07. Central charge c = 3L/2G_N; only the 2D vacuum and BTZ geometries are treated.

fig37_scrambling_otoc_entanglement.name: fig37_scrambling_otoc_entanglement
fig37_scrambling_otoc_entanglement.caption: Haar-random two-qubit brickwork circuits. (a) The OTOC F = Re Tr[W(t)^dag V^dag W(t) V]/d between Z on site 0 and Z at the stated distance stays at 1 until the operator front arrives and then decays toward ~0 (mean over 24 circuits, bands +/- 2 s.e.m.). (b) The arrival layer grows linearly with distance, a discrete light cone (open boundary conditions, so edge effects exist). (c) Half-chain entanglement from a product state saturates at 3.650 +/- 0.002 versus the Page value 3.659. Exact state-vector calculations; small sizes only.

fig38_quantum_error_correction.name: fig38_quantum_error_correction
fig38_quantum_error_correction.caption: (a) Monte Carlo logical failure of the 3-qubit repetition code under independent bit flips (agrees with 3p^2 - 2p^3) and the 5-qubit perfect code under independent depolarising noise (failure ~ O(p^2)); points with zero observed failures are omitted; counts are over 6000 trials, binomial error ~ sqrt(f(1-f)/6000). (b) Coherent-information-style diagnostic I(ref:kept) for a maximally entangled reference: the 5-qubit code keeps the logical qubit recoverable (2 ln 2) after erasing any 2 qubits and loses it at 3, matching its distance 3; the repetition code protects only against X errors and is not an erasure-correcting code for quantum information. (c) Worst-case recoverability. This is a finite-code toy analogue of subregion reconstruction in holography, not a derivation of it.
